column4: Internet traffic reaches a control zone
column6: Control and supervisory systems are exchanging traffic directly with internet addresses. Nothing in Levels 0–2 should have a path to or from the internet; that is the single most exploited OT exposure.
column7: Block the path at the zone boundary firewall, or document it as an allowed conduit limited to the specific hosts and ports shown. Route anything that must cross IT/OT through the DMZ.
column8: IEC 62443-3-3 SR 5.1, SR 1.13 · ATT&CK T0883 Internet Accessible Device, T0822 External Remote Services · M0930, M0937

column4: Internet traffic reaches the operations zone without passing through a DMZ
column6: Level 3 systems are talking straight to the internet. Anything that needs outside access (patches, cloud historians, vendor support) should be brokered by a server in the industrial DMZ.
column7: Block the path at the zone boundary firewall, or document it as an allowed conduit limited to the specific hosts and ports shown. Route anything that must cross IT/OT through the DMZ.

column4: Devices in the traffic that aren't in the Nmap scan
column6: These addresses exchanged traffic during the capture but did not answer the scan. They may be transient laptops, unmanaged devices, or something that should not be on the network at all.
column7: Identify the owner of each device. Enforce port security / 802.1X on control-network switches and keep a current asset register.
column8: IEC 62443-3-3 SR 7.8 · ATT&CK T0864 Transient Cyber Asset, T0848 Rogue Master · M0930

column4: Port-scan pattern seen in the traffic
column6: A host opened many short connections to different hosts and ports. If this isn't a scheduled, approved scan, it is reconnaissance, and active scanning can crash fragile controllers.
column7: Confirm whether the scan was authorised. Restrict which hosts may initiate connections into control zones and alert on scan patterns at the boundary.
column8: ATT&CK T0846 Remote System Discovery, T0846.001 Port Scan · M0930, M0937

column4: Remote-access sessions into control zones that don't come from the DMZ
column6: Interactive access (RDP, VNC, SSH, Telnet, remote-support tools) into Levels 0–2 should arrive through a single remote-access gateway in the DMZ with MFA, recording and time-limited approval.
column7: Terminate vendor and engineer access on a DMZ jump host or secure remote-access gateway, require MFA, and block RDP/VNC/SSH into control zones from anywhere else.
column8: IEC 62443-3-3 SR 1.13, SR 2.6 · ATT&CK T0886 Remote Services, T0822 · M0932, M0935

column4: Cleartext management traffic crosses into control zones
column6: Telnet, FTP, HTTP and SNMPv1/v2c send credentials and community strings in the clear. Carried across a zone boundary, they can be captured anywhere along the path.
column7: Switch to SSH, HTTPS and SNMPv3, or keep device management inside a dedicated management zone instead of crossing production conduits.
column8: IEC 62443-3-3 SR 4.1, SR 1.5 · ATT&CK T0859 Valid Accounts, T1694.001 Default Credentials · M0942

column4: Windows file sharing / RPC crosses into control zones
column6: SMB and MS-RPC are the main way ransomware and worms move laterally. They should not cross from operations or IT into supervisory and control zones.
column7: Block 135/139/445 at the boundary. Move file transfers to a DMZ file-transfer server or an approved one-way mechanism.
column8: IEC 62443-3-3 SR 5.1 · ATT&CK T0866 Exploitation of Remote Services · M0930, M0937

column4: Windows / IT hosts inside a Level 0–1 zone
column6: Hosts with Windows file sharing, RDP or VNC sit on the same segment as controllers. They are the usual stepping stone into a control cell.
column7: Move workstations and servers to Level 2 or 3, or harden them (disable SMB/RDP) if they must stay in the cell.

column5: Site Operations → Line 2 Packaging (S7comm / IEC 61850 MMS, OPC UA, Omron FINS, MELSEC MC, SNMP); Site Operations → Line 1 Filling (EtherNet/IP, SNMP); Site Operations → Utilities (Modbus/TCP); Line 2 Packaging → Site Operations (NTP)
column6: Level 3 systems (often OPC servers or historians) talk straight to controllers. This is common and can be acceptable, but each path should be documented and limited to the specific hosts and protocols involved.
column7: Block the path at the zone boundary firewall, or document it as an allowed conduit limited to the specific hosts and ports shown. Route anything that must cross IT/OT through the DMZ.

column4: Converged hosts expose both OT and IT services
column6: These hosts offer an industrial protocol and Windows services at the same time, so one compromise reaches both sides. Common for SCADA and OPC servers; worth hardening.
column7: Disable services the host doesn't need and restrict which zones may reach each service.

column4: Telnet or FTP open on control devices
column6: Cleartext management services on controllers are a frequent source of default and hard-coded credential exposure.
column7: Turn off Telnet and FTP where the device allows it; otherwise restrict them to a management host.
column8: IEC 62443-3-3 SR 4.1 · ATT&CK T1694.001 Default Credentials · M0942
